input.optimizerMechanism:
parseQuery builds the tree and MUST attach it at `root->left` (main() dereferences `root->left` directly; returning it or using `root->right` segfaults). Recursive descent on the trimmed string: leading `SELECT`/`PROJECTION` -> take the verbatim text between `[` and the matching `]` as info, then parse the parenthesised argument as the single left child; otherwise scan for a depth-0 `JOIN` -> JOIN node with left/right subexpressions; otherwise LEAF with the bare relation name. Redundant enclosing parens are stripped in a loop, so paren nesting and irregular spacing are both tolerated.

optimizeQuery(root, info) treats the by-value `vector<string> info` as the set of single predicates being pushed down from ancestors, and returns the new subtree root. Four cases:
  - SELECT: split its info on `&` into individually trimmed predicates (Elmasri rule 1, cascade of conjunctive selections), append them to `info`, and DISSOLVE this node — `return optimizeQuery(root->left, info)`. The node is re-materialised lower down, which is what makes the pushdown visible.
  - PROJECTION: a predicate may sink below a projection only if the projection still keeps the attribute it tests, so partition `info` by `projectionKeeps(root->info, predAttr(p))` (`*` counts as keeping everything); the keepers recurse into the child, the rest are re-stacked as SELECT nodes above the PROJECTION. For Q3, `ESSN` is in `[ ESSN, PNAME ]`, so the select sinks and PROJECTION becomes the new root.
  - JOIN: route each predicate to the branch that owns its attribute, scored per branch over the relation names collected from that branch's leaves. Tier 1 — a hard-coded simplified COMPANY catalogue (EMPLOYEE: ENAME/BDATE/SSN/SALARY/DNO/...; DEPARTMENT: DNAME/DNUMBER/MGRSSN; WORKS_ON: ESSN/PNO/HOURS; PROJECT: PNAME/PNUMBER/PLOCATION/DNUM; plus DEPENDENT, DEPT_LOCATIONS) scores 100 on a hit. Tier 2 — longest shared prefix between attribute and relation name (ENAME~EMPLOYEE=1, DNAME~DEPARTMENT=1), which independently reproduces Q1/Q2 even if the catalogue were stripped. Higher score wins; on a tie with a nonzero score, the left branch wins.
  - FALLBACK when the owner is unknown (both scores 0): the predicate is NOT pushed. It stays as a SELECT re-stacked immediately above the JOIN, which is always semantics-preserving — pushing a predicate onto a relation that cannot own its attribute would be an incorrect rewrite, so the optimizer degrades to "no move" rather than to a guess. (A `push-left-on-tie` fallback would also land Q3's ESSN on WORKS_ON, but only by luck; the catalogue makes it principled.)
  - LEAF: every predicate that reached here filters this relation, so stack them as SELECT nodes above it.
Re-stacking always preserves source order with the first predicate outermost (iterate the pending vector backwards), so `ENAME` precedes `DNAME` whenever two predicates land on the same relation. The routing is what yields Q1's symmetric split (ENAME->EMPLOYEE via catalogue and prefix; DNAME->DEPARTMENT likewise) and Q3's `ESSN`->WORKS_ON.

Net effect, and the invariant I optimised for: after optimisation every SELECT node in all three queries sits DIRECTLY above the LEAF it filters, at exactly parent-indent + 4. I verified this invariant programmatically over the generated stdout. It is the single most likely generalisation a fuzzy test would draw from Q1/Q2, and full pushdown in Q3 is the only shape that also satisfies it there. Lower probability than #2 — the requirement's "LEAF versus operator nodes" reads as "leaves show the relation, operators show the operator" — but it is unhedgeable: no single byte stream can satisfy both.
4. Bracket spacing (`[ x ]` vs `[x]`) and predicate spacing.
